La DAL, le goût de la solidarité aliment: La DAL, a Taste of Food Solidarity
Pour La DAL, l’objectif est de retirer l: For La DAL, the goal is to take money out of the equation as much as possible when it comes to access to good food.
Dimitri Espérance, co-fondateur de la DA: Dimitri Espérance, co-founder of La DAL. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
À Saint-Henri, les résidants du quartier: In Saint-Henri, residents have no shortage of restaurants to choose from. But for many, when it comes to cooking at home, things get complicated. This is especially true for those who don’t live near one of the three big grocery stores, which are concentrated in a single spot and serve the whole neighbourhood. That is where La Démarche alimentaire locale (DAL) chose to step in, founding a self-managed grocery store that opened its doors last February.
Dans le petit commerce de quartier, on t: In this small neighbourhood shop, you can find everything: fresh fruits and vegetables, dairy products, condiments and spices, but also good cheer and light. Residents are starting to discover the store and do their shopping there, which gives the collective the time it needs to make adjustments.
« La DAL est un collectif citoyen de Sai: “La DAL is a citizen collective in Saint-Henri that wants to tackle food insecurity, particularly in the western part of the neighbourhood,” explains Dimitri Espérance, co-founder and executive director of the collective. The grocer, who has lived in the neighbourhood for six years, knows well what makes it beautiful and what makes residents’ daily lives harder. So in 2019, he decided to go out and meet his neighbours to better understand their food needs and get their impressions of the effects of COVID, through a vox pop and a petition. “The lack of access to food and fresh produce is a frustration many people live with,” says the social innovation consultant.
La DAL n’est pas la première initiative: La DAL is not the neighbourhood’s first food initiative – there is notably the <l1>Frigo Communautaire de Saint-Henri</l1> – but with this project, Espérance wants to reach the general public. The goal is not only to help people eat well, but also to let residents of the neighbourhood build ties with one another, as neighbours. Bit by bit, the idea of setting up a self-managed grocery store took shape. It is a market that runs thanks to the involvement of its members. Each member must do three hours of volunteer work at the store every month in exchange for a member discount. Anyone, however, can shop there. “The discount allows us to keep prices affordable for non-members,” the founder explains. He discovered self-managed grocery stores at a conference, notably Park Slope Food Coop in Brooklyn. Active since the 1970s, it serves 16,000 members – almost the same number as the entire population of Saint-Henri. The place is run by its consumers, who put in a few hours a month, and only members can shop there. La DAL chose to adapt this model to residents’ realities, adopting a system inspired by the co-op. “A co-op is more complicated to set up. Legally, it has to charge its members a fee, what’s called a ‘membership share.’ That’s a barrier we didn’t want to have,” Dimitri explains.
Si Saint-Henri est historiquement popula: While Saint-Henri has historically been a working-class neighbourhood, it continues to undergo radical change. In its latest census of the neighbourhood, conducted in 2016, Statistics Canada reported that rents in Saint-Henri had risen by 22% since 2011. It also noted an 8.7% increase in the number of condos, compared with 3.2% in the rest of the island of Montréal. “Gentrification is the cause of a certain erosion of social ties between newcomers and longtime residents,” observes Espérance, who wants to bridge that gap. “We’re trying to create a place where everyone has the chance to be in contact.”
Malgré l’embourgeoisement rapide qui sév: Despite the rapid gentrification that has plagued the neighbourhood for several years, no other grocery store has opened in Saint-Henri – La DAL is the first to set up shop there in 25 years. As Dimitri Espérance explains, a so-called disadvantaged neighbourhood is not necessarily a food desert, while an affluent area can be one. The problem in Saint-Henri is well known, and not new, but its causes – and solutions – are rarely discussed. “A food desert is not a natural phenomenon that happens by chance in a place. There is a historical, social and economic context that explains it; it’s not a situation that resolves itself naturally,” says Espérance. The neighbourhood’s deindustrialization, which has been going on since the 1970s, has helped impoverish it, causing food infrastructure to decline. In recent years, many commercial spaces have been converted to residential use, a more profitable approach for landlords. Over the past year, in fact, two convenience stores have closed, and their spaces are slated to become housing. And because of COVID, several restaurants have also closed. One might think gentrification would be an incentive to open a grocery store, but according to Dimitri Espérance, that has not been the case. Owners of commercial spaces tend to favour certain types of businesses, especially if they don’t live in the neighbourhood and don’t see the point of living there. “Landlords see [grocery stores] as a nuisance: there are a lot of deliveries, they generate waste, and so on,” he says. Before the pandemic, many commercial spaces on Notre-Dame Street sat vacant; the majority of them are now rented or being renovated.
Voilà pourquoi il a fallu un bon moment: That is why it took La DAL a good while to find a space, and major renovations were then needed to welcome people and bring light to the small neighbourhood grocery store. At the outset, the collective wanted to reclaim a long-unoccupied former fire station and give it back to residents. After the City refused, the collective had to look for another location, still with the goal of opening a community food centre.
La COVID est également venue aggraver le: COVID also made needs worse. Given how little food infrastructure the neighbourhood has, the situation became such that enormous lineups formed outside the few establishments. “Living in a food desert during lockdown becomes serious,” the grocer says. After a long process, La DAL thus came to act concretely where no one had done so in years. “We’re happy to be arriving in the neighbourhood with this offer,” says Dimitri. “Without the Frigo Communautaire and without La DAL, the neighbourhood would have become unliveable for many people.”
<strong>De la justice alimentaire à l’éc: From food justice to the social economy
Qu’est-ce que l’insécurité alimentaire ?: What is food insecurity? “It is a state in which a person, or a group of people, finds themselves when the availability of healthy and nutritious food, or the ability to acquire personally satisfactory food through socially acceptable means, is limited or uncertain,” reads the Government of Quebec’s website. Here is how Espérance describes food security: “A person who is at all times able to find, nearby, food that is healthy and tied to their cultural habits.”
Au Québec, ce sont 17 % des ménages qui: In Quebec, 17% of households are food insecure – a situation made worse by the pandemic. At La DAL, food is a universal right. “The government isn’t doing enough for this fundamental right to be respected,” Espérance believes. He cites food banks as an example, where you have to prove your right to use the service, notably by providing proof of income. “In Quebec, we often see a Judeo-Christian version of charity: when a person experiences insecurity, it’s treated as something individual, and they have to be saved,” he notes, adding that he thinks cities like Toronto have a more intersectional view of the issue.
La DAL met ainsi de l’avant le concept d: La DAL thus puts forward the concept of food justice, approaching food from a systemic perspective. The aim is to take into account the exclusions it creates, the people it leaves behind and those who profit from the system. “For example, there is solidarity with local producers so that they can earn a decent income, enough for them to not simply survive,” he illustrates.
C’est en 2019, alors en arrêt de travail: It was in 2019, while on leave from work, that the social innovation consultant got his start in food farming. His discoveries influenced the project that was to come. “There’s often a lack of historical perspective on these things,” he says, explaining certain concepts that are now growing ever more popular. “Permaculture, for example, is an appropriation of ancestral Indigenous and African techniques. Our communities have long been used to practising urban agriculture as a way to ensure food autonomy. Now it’s white people who are being put in the spotlight,” he says. The same goes for food co-ops, which La DAL draws on. “In North America, it’s mostly Black communities that came together to increase their purchasing power and be more autonomous. These are things we’ve done for generations, because we had no choice,” he says.
Pour lancer une telle entreprise d’écono: To launch such a social economy enterprise, the grocer had to overcome many challenges. “As a racialized person deciding to create an organization in the food insecurity sector, which is very white, and where racialized people are more often beneficiaries than leaders, it was hard to establish myself,” Dimitri Espérance confides, in a neighbourhood where the proportion of racialized people is below the Montréal average. He also had to gain recognition from the other players in the neighbourhood, elected officials and residents, on top of seeking funding, finding a space in a very competitive market and handling all the bureaucracy surrounding the operation of a non-profit, including obtaining permits.
Autrement, l’avenir de La DAL s’annonce: Otherwise, La DAL’s future looks promising or, at the very least, delicious. The collective is setting up a pilot project in collaboration with the Sud-Ouest borough, in which prepared meals will be made available to seniors’ residences, in addition to being sold at the grocery store. Despite wearing so many hats, Dimitri Espérance stays calm. “I’ve been thinking of myself as a grocer for a while now,” he says as new members join La DAL. “The challenge is mostly getting members to come in and to see themselves as grocers; it’s ongoing training.”
S’il a un conseil à donner à ceux qui vo: If he has one piece of advice for those who would like to embark on such an adventure, it is to know your community very well. “I’m a new resident of Saint-Henri, and there are people who have been here for generations,” he points out. So La DAL’s activities over its first six months consisted of going out to meet people in the neighbourhood, building relationships and talking with them. “We had to see whether the perspective we had on Saint-Henri’s food desert was shared. We did everything to make sure our problem was extremely well defined.
Quand on a eu cette confirmation, on s’e: When we got that confirmation, we felt much more comfortable launching the project,” says Dimitri. The young entrepreneur felt supported by the community in the face of obstacles, but also in each of his successes. Having never worked in a grocery store, he went to “learn the ropes” – that is, to get informed, receive a mentor’s advice and work – at <l1>Le Détour</l1>, a self-managed grocery store in Pointe-Saint-Charles, at <l2>Le Dépôt</l2>, a community food centre in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, at the grocery store Les Récoltes in Rosemont, and at the zero-waste grocery stores <l3>LOCO</l3>. “It’s all well and good to have citizens becoming grocers, but you also have to realize that, romanticism aside, it’s a lot of work to acquire the skills you don’t have,” he says, keeping his feet on the ground. And now it’s his turn to inspire others. “I realized that, even though that’s not at all why I did it, I had the chance to be a role model for people,” he says humbly.
Si j’avais vu une personne noire ou raci: If I had seen a Black or racialized person at the head of a food-based social organization, maybe I would have taken the leap sooner.” His second piece of advice is aimed instead at those who are like him. “Don’t focus on what people think you should do,” he urges. That is what happened when he started La DAL. “It didn’t go the way we wanted,” he recalls. “But we wanted it to be a grand project. And starting small doesn’t stop us from thinking big.”
